subject: How to understand two terms in one f()? like f(ID.area, year, model='...')

messages.author: ff1a5632abbf2fe9
messages.subject: How to understand two terms in one f()? like f(ID.area, year, model='...')
parts:
Hi,

I read two papers with R code from your team. In the specification of interaction of space and time, one linf of code is like the following:

formula.ST1<- y ~ 1 + f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) + f(ID.area1,year,model="iid") + (year-mean(year))

The paper explains year as the weight.

Meanwhile, another line of code for the interaction of nonspatial and nontemporal effects

# the ID.area.year variable is a generated vector, which is from 1 to year*ID.area
formula.ST3<- y ~ 1 + f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) + f(ID.year,model="rw1") + f(ID.year1,model="iid") + f(ID.area.year,model="iid") 

Constrasting formula.ST1 with formula.ST3, I have two following questions；

1) In formula.ST1, What is the year weighting for?

2) The specification of interaction has nothing to do with the number of terms in f(), does it? A naive thought would be: there should be an interaction effect in the formula.ST1 (two terms in one f()), while there is no interaction effect in the formula.ST3(every f() just has one term)

Thanks
Xing

messages.author: b453c29749de564d
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to understand two terms in one f()? like f(ID.area, year, model='...')
parts:
all f() models has as the first argument, the index within the model and
an optional second argument which is the weight.

if x is the f() model, then f(idx,...) gives contribution

x[idx[i]]

to the i'th linear predictor.

with

f(idx,w, ...)

then the contribution is

x[idx[i]] * w[i]

so by default, w[] = 1.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to understand two terms in one f()? like f(ID.area, year, model='...')
parts:
This is a general property of linear models, and not specific to R-INLA,
but basically this is the situation:

For any covariate with values x_i, any model of the form
a + x_i*b
can be rewritten as
(a+m*b) + (x_i-m)*b
where m is an arbitrary constant, reparameterised into
alpha + z_i*b
where z_i is a shifted version of the covariate.
Note that the structure of the model did not change, but the values of
the a and alpha parameters are not the same, but they are related via
the value of m and the b parameter.
It is common to center the x_i covariate by choosing m=mean(x_i) (or
some other value that will act as the new "origin" for the covariate),
since this makes alpha and b less correlated than a and b would be, in
the posterior distribution, and it also improves the numerical
properties of the model. When doing a fully Bayesian analysis with
vague priors on the parameters the difference is in theory small, but in
practice centering can be useful. E.g., due to the reduced correlation,
the posterior marginal distributions for alpha and b are intuitively
easier to interpret than the posterior marginals for a and b.

This should be covered in any decent textbook on linear models (the
frequentistic version of these models tend to use centering even more
than Bayesian methods, so there should be plenty to read). One just
needs to keep in mind what the interpretation of the intercept parameter
(a and alpha, respectively) is in the different models.

In your case, I'd suggest replacing 2000,2001,2002 by -1,0,1, so that
the intercept parameter becomes the average effect over the three years
(with 1,2,3 instead of -1,0,1 the intercept would try to capture the
effect for year 1999, which is a bit odd in terms of interpretation...)

Finn L

As Håvard explained, when there are two terms in one f(), say f(ID.area, year, model='...'), the 'year' is a weight to the 'ID.area'

Yes, i simplified the model Quite a bit to get to the core of the issue, sorry about that.  To get your model from mine, both the a/alpha and the x/z/b terms need their own f() function, where the first have no weights and is identical for the three timepoints and the second used x/z as weights.  But the basic principle is mostly the same.  You need to think in terms of what the mathematical model is before thinking about specific R -implementation...

Finn
